variants.name: Anxious tech skeptics, wary of others
variants.text: These respondents combine guarded trust in people with low confidence in institutions and mounting unease about automation. They tend to rate robots and AI as uncomfortable or worrying, while still holding a generally satisfied view of how democracy works. Their answers on social trust, institutional trust, and technology cluster together, forming a cautious, skeptical outlook that is not outright pessimistic about daily life.

variants.name: Content middle-class, routine-leaning family people
variants.text: These respondents describe their finances as stable, their life as fairly routine, and their happiness as high, with family and social contact fairly frequent. Views on the economy and taxes often run negative while personal finances feel steady, so they separate private contentment from public gloom. Their answers on social life, work-family tension, and personal satisfaction move together, showing a settled, family-centred orientation.

variants.name: Politically detached yet trusting realists
variants.text: These respondents show low to moderate political interest and mixed satisfaction with democratic processes, while often verifying political information online. Their trust in others and their views on technology lean toward the middle or mildly positive, with few extreme ratings. Answers on civic engagement, economic outlook, and emerging technology tend to hover around neutral, producing a measured but noncommittal profile.

variant_stats.name: Anxious tech skeptics, wary of others

variants.name: Disengaged, financially strained, routine lives
variants.text: Respondents feel their finances are stuck below average and unchanged, tend to see the economy as poor and taxes as too heavy, and describe life as routine rather than exciting. They are not very happy overall, yet they are only moderately satisfied with their finances, so their dissatisfaction is mild rather than acute. Political interest is absent, and they rarely check political claims, so their outlook on public affairs is passive and detached.

variants.name: Withdrawn social life, wary of technology
variants.text: Respondents socialize occasionally with friends outside their neighborhood but seldom see relatives, and they do not report family sacrifices at work. Their views lean toward traditional family expectations about men's work. On technology they are neutral in general but express strong worry about artificial intelligence and rate automation of many human tasks at middling-to-moderate levels, which together suggest guarded, uneasy modernity.

variants.name: Skeptical of spending, unsure of progress
variants.text: Respondents combine a neutral stance on technology with real unease about AI and a belief that science receives too much public money. Their financial self-assessment is steady rather than improving, and they see their social standing as working class. Taken together, the answers form a picture of people who feel stuck, distrust large institutions and expensive ambitions, and do not expect things to get better soon.

Skeptical of spending, unsure of progress

variants.name: Trusting, politically engaged, dissatisfied
variants.text: Respondents combine high generalized and institutional trust with intense political interest and active information-checking, yet remain dissatisfied with how democracy works. Their trust in people and institutions runs high even as they express frustration with the political system, and they verify political claims often rather than accepting them passively.

variants.name: Content and financially comfortable, yet dull
variants.text: These people report improving finances, middle-class self-placement, and very good views of the economy and their own happiness, but describe daily life as routine or dull. They socialize frequently with friends and relatives, and they feel taxes are too low, suggesting a comfortable, settled outlook that lacks excitement.

variant_stats.name: Content and financially comfortable, yet dull

variants.name: Contented, politically engaged affluent
variants.text: Respondents feel very happy and pleased with democracy and the economy, follow politics closely, and see their finances as improving while their income sits well above typical levels. They consider themselves upper class yet find day-to-day life fairly routine, and they resist taxes as too heavy while still wanting more public spending on science.

variants.name: Insular routine with strong ties
variants.text: These respondents are satisfied and happy overall but experience life as routine rather than exciting. They rarely socialize with friends outside their neighborhood or with extended relatives, yet they report adjusting work commitments for family, and they feel neutral about the claim that work crowds out family life.

variants.name: Prosperous skeptics of taxation
variants.text: Respondents combine rising personal finances and high confidence in the economy with a firm sense that government takes too much of their income. Their self-placement in the top class, comfortable life satisfaction, and call for greater investment in research form a pattern of confident, growth-minded optimism about the country.

variants.name: Trusting institutions, wary of people
variants.text: Respondents hold a guarded view of other people, believing one can't be too careful, yet place strong confidence in public institutions and in how democracy works. Their trust is directed at systems rather than individuals, and they actively verify political information they encounter.

variants.name: Contented, routine-anchored family life
variants.text: These respondents feel financially stable and see their economic situation as unchanged, describing themselves as very happy while still finding life exciting. Their social world is anchored by frequent time with relatives and less frequent contact with friends outside the neighborhood, and they hold traditional views on family and work.

variants.name: Enthusiastic about science, ambivalent about machines
variants.text: Respondents combine strong pro-technology attitudes and support for more scientific funding with discomfort about robots and AI taking over human tasks. Their optimism about technology's general value sits alongside a clear reluctance to hand over particular responsibilities to automated systems.
